as_written_in_papers.quote: |  | SLC2A10 c.509G>A | 20q13.12 | 606145 | NM_030777.3 | p.Trp170Ter | Hz | Nonsense/Pathogenic | new | ATORS |
The second detected heterozygous mutation c.509G>A, p.(Trp170Ter) in the SLC2A10 gene is a new stop-gain (nonsense) variant, which has not been reported in the literature.

cases.statement: One person: P10 (D.N.B.), a male first evaluated at 3 months and re-evaluated at 1 year, carrying c.509G>A together with c.394C>T p.(Arg132Trp) in SLC2A10 (reported as compound heterozygous). Features: arterial tortuosity of the aorta and its large branches on aortography, aortic coarctation/arch hypoplasia, aortic regurgitation, septal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, skin laxity, joint hypermobility, inguinal-scrotal hernia, congenital clubfoot, craniofacial dysmorphism.

people.label: P10
people.zygosity_or_genotype: compound heterozygous as stated in the text (Table 2 lists each variant as 'Hz'); phase not confirmed by parental testing
people.key_phenotypes: arterial tortuosity of the aorta and all large arteries; cardiovascular anomalies (septal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, aortic coarctation, aortic regurgitation; Table 3 also lists aortic arch hypoplasia, LV diastolic dysfunction, pulmonary artery stenosis); skin laxity/hyperextensibility; joint hypermobility; inguinal-scrotal hernia; congenital clubfoot; craniofacial dysmorphism

quotes.quote: | P10 (D.N.B) | 3 m | M | - | AAH, LVDD, AI, LVH, PAS, ATORS | - | - | + | LH | - | Inguinal–scrotal hernia, SH |  | ATORS |

The last patient (P10, D.N.B., male) was initially evaluated at the age of 3 months and then re-evaluated at the age of 1 year, and he presented skin laxity, joint hypermobility, inguinal–scrotal hernia, congenital clubfoot, and craniofacial dysmorphism associated with cardiovascular anomalies (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, predominantly septal, aortic coarctation, and aortic regurgitation).

Aortography revealed significant tortuosity of the aorta along its entire length, as well as of all the large arteries emerging from it, raising the suspicion of the diagnosis of arterial tortuosity syndrome (ATORS).
Genetic testing (Illumina TruSight Cardio Sequencing Panel) identified two mutations (compound heterozygous status) in the SLC2A10 gene located on chromosome 20q13.12 (Table 2).
The first is a heterozygous missense variant c.394C>T, p.(Arg132Trp) in the SLC2A10 gene affecting a well-conserved nucleotide.

phenotype_specificity.statement: The person's features (generalized arterial tortuosity, aortic coarctation, pulmonary artery stenosis, skin hyperextensibility, joint hypermobility, hernia, craniofacial dysmorphism) overlap the paper's own description of ATORS. Testing was a 174-gene cardiac panel that includes other aortopathy/connective tissue genes (FBN1, TGFBR1, TGFBR2, COL3A1 and others); the paper does not state explicitly that these other genes were negative in P10, though only the two SLC2A10 variants are listed for him. Ophthalmological and orthopedic evaluations are stated to have excluded other ATORS-associated anomalies (i.e. a statement about further features, not about alternative causes).

quotes.quote: ATORS is associated with the elongation, tortuosity, and aneurysms of the large and medium arteries with craniofacial dysmorphism (long face, hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, beaked nose, sagging cheeks, a high palate, and micrognathia), skin (soft and hyperextensible skin, cutis laxa, and hernias), skeletal (joint hypermobility and congenital contractures), and ocular (keratoconus) manifestations and generalized hypotonia.
The cardiovascular abnormalities include pulmonary and aortic stenosis, coarctation of the aorta, abnormal implantation of the aortic branches, and an increased risk of ischemic events [32].
This panel also includes candidate genes for aortopathies and EDS: ACTA2, COL3A1, COL5A1, COL5A2, EFEMP2, ELN, FBN1, FBN2, MYH1, MYLK, SLC2A10, SMADTGFB2, TGFB3, TGFBR1, and TGFBR2.
The multidisciplinary management also included ophthalmological and orthopedic evaluations, which excluded other anomalies associated with ATORS.

segregation.statement: No segregation data reported. Family history of aortic disease is marked absent for P10 in Table 3. First-degree relatives were evaluated clinically and by imaging and genetic testing was recommended, but no relative's genotype or phenotype result is reported.

quotes.quote: Also, the patient’s first-degree relatives were evaluated clinically and by echocardiography, MRA, and/or CT scan, and genetic testing was recommended.

de_novo.statement: Parents were not tested according to the results section; the paper says parental testing 'will be necessary'. The abstract nevertheless describes one of the two SLC2A10 variants as 'de novo' (presumably the new variant c.509G>A, since c.394C>T is called 'known'). This is an internal contradiction; no parental genotypes or parentage confirmation are reported.

quotes.quote: In the performed sequencing, four of the reads contained both variants and the results suggested that they are positioned in trans (on different chromosomes), but for certainty, testing of the patient’s parents will be necessary.

Two other pathogenic heterozygous variants (one de novo and the other a known mutation) in the SLC2A10 gene (compound heterozygous genotype) were identified in a patient diagnosed with arterial tortuosity syndrome (ATORS).

in_trans.statement: Other allele: c.394C>T, p.(Arg132Trp) (NM_030777.3), described as known and reported in other ATORS patients. Phase was not shown by parental testing; the authors infer trans from sequencing reads ('four of the reads contained both variants') and describe the variants as 'most likely in trans'.

quotes.quote: | P10 (D.N.B) | SLC2A10 c.394C>T | 20q13.12 | 606145 | NM_030777.3 | p.Arg132Trp | Hz | Missense/Pathogenic | known | ATORS |

In another patient (P10, D.N.B), two heterozygous mutations (one missense, pathogenic variant and the other a pathogenic nonsense variant, most likely in trans) were detected in the SLC2A10 gene associated with ATORS (Figure 2).

In the performed sequencing, four of the reads contained both variants and the results suggested that they are positioned in trans (on different chromosomes), but for certainty, testing of the patient’s parents will be necessary.
The missense variant was reported in individuals with autosomal recessive ATORS (PMID: 17935213, 28726533, 29543232) [85,86,87].

variant_type_and_mechanism.statement: c.509G>A is predicted to create a premature stop codon, p.(Trp170Ter) (nonsense). The paper states that other nonsense variants in SLC2A10 cause ATORS and that SLC2A10 encodes GLUT10, which regulates TGF-beta signaling; it makes no explicit loss-of-function or nonsense-mediated decay statement for this variant.

quotes.quote: Other nonsense variants are reported to be pathogenic, representing a cause of ATORS.
Pathogenic variants of the SLC2A10 gene, which encodes the GLUT10 protein that regulates the TGF-β signaling pathway, cause arterial tortuosity syndrome (ATORS; OMIM #208050, ORPHA:3342).

computational_predictions.statement: The authors report that LRT and MutationTaster predict a deleterious effect; no scores given.

quotes.quote: In silico prediction models (LRT and MutationTaster) predict that the SLC2A10 c.509G>A, p.(Trp170Ter) variant has a deleterious effect on the protein.

population_data_in_papers.statement: The authors state the variant has not been reported in large populations (no database or frequency named).

quotes.quote: The variant has not been reported in large populations nor in other patients with ATORS in the literature.

authors_classification.statement: The authors classify c.509G>A as pathogenic according to ACMG guidelines (no criterion codes given); Table 2 lists it as 'Nonsense/Pathogenic', 'new'.

quotes.quote: For these reasons, the SLC2A10 c.509G>A variant was classified as pathogenic according to the ACMG guidelines.

concerns: Single paper, single person (P10); no segregation, no functional data.

Paper contradicts itself on inheritance: the abstract calls one SLC2A10 variant 'de novo', while the results state that parental testing has not yet been done ('testing of the patient's parents will be necessary'). Table 2 labels c.509G>A 'new' (not previously reported), which may be the source of the 'de novo' wording.

Phase evidence is ambiguous: the authors say 'four of the reads contained both variants' yet conclude the variants are in trans. Reads carrying both variant alleles would ordinarily suggest cis; the panel should treat phase as unconfirmed.
Zygosity column in Table 2 gives 'Hz' (heterozygous) for each variant separately; compound heterozygosity is the authors' interpretation in the text.
Paper's transcript is NM_030777.3; batch HGVS uses NM_030777.4. Protein check agrees (p.Trp170Ter).
Panel (174 genes) included other aortopathy genes, but the paper does not explicitly state negative results for them in P10.
The paper's text and Table 3 describe P10's cardiac findings in different terms (text: septal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, aortic coarctation, aortic regurgitation; Table 3: AAH, LVDD, AI, LVH, PAS).
notes_for_panel: Evidence comes from one case series of ten syndromic HTAD patients from Romania (PMID 39456956), in which P10 is the only ATORS case. The variant is a nonsense change found with c.394C>T p.(Arg132Trp), which the authors describe as previously reported in ATORS. Parents were not tested, so both phase and the abstract's 'de novo' claim are unverified.
